title: The Fan and the Falling Tears
story:
Krishna read the change in the air before anyone spoke of it. Narada was still seated with Rukmini, the sage's voice still praising the flower, but one face was missing from the circle of his wives, and he knew, as he knew everything, where it had gone. Under some pretext he rose and left the festival.

His steps carried him quickly toward the spacious mansion on the Raivataka hills that Vishvakarma himself had built for Satyabhama. He was aware, as he walked, that the daughter of Satrajit — dearer to him than his own vital breaths — was under the influence of jealous resentment, and the slayer of Madhu went the slower for it, with greater fear. He left Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada, told his servant Daruka to wait at the gate, and entered the palace alone.

From a distance he saw her, inside the apartment of anger, in the midst of her handmaids, sighing hot and frequently. She laughed a derisive laugh mixed with sighs at a lotus she had brought near her own lotus-like face and was nipping with her nails. Sometimes she described figures on the ground with the tip of her slightly bent toe. Sometimes she sat in deep thought, her face resting on her left palm. Sometimes she took the sandal from her maids' hands, smeared it on her breast, and then cruelly threw it aside. She rose from her bed and fell into it again. He watched all of this — the theater of a woman who wanted to be angry at the one man she loved — and did not announce himself.

Then she laid her head on her pillow, drawing her veil over her face, and Krishna thought: this is my opportunity. By signs he commanded the handmaids not to speak of him. With faltering steps he approached Satyabhama, took up the fan, and standing by her side began to fan slowly, and to laugh gently.

His contact with the Parijata flower had perfumed him, and the fragrance spread through the chamber — divine, supernatural, rare. Satyabhama smelled it and was taken with admiration. She uncovered her face. "What is this?" Rising from her bed, without bestowing a single glance on her godly husband, she began to question her maids about the cause of the fragrance. The maids could say nothing; they knelt on the ground with their faces to the earth and their palms joined in supplication. Not finding the source, Satyabhama wondered whether the earth herself had emitted one of her excellent scents. Then, looking on all sides, her glance suddenly lighted on Kesava, the creator of the worlds.

"Ah! right," she said — and suddenly her eyes were dimmed with tears, the intensity of love filling her all the more with jealous anger. With her delicate lips pouting and herself sighing, she turned her downcast countenance away in another direction and remained so for a while. Then, contracting her brows in a disapproving frown and placing her face on her palms, she said to Hari with her eyes upraised: "Thou lookest beautiful." The tears of jealous passion flowed down from her eyes like drops of dew falling from a pair of lotus petals.

The lotus-eyed Krishna, seeing the tears stream down his wife's lotus-like face, approached her in haste and held them in his hands. Wiping with his own hands the tears that were falling on her breast, the wearer of the Srivatsa mark spoke gently. Why did tears flow from her eyes like dew from a pair of lotuses? Why did her face and body wear the look of the full moon in the morning sky, or the full-blown lotus at noon? Why, today, did she wear plain white garments and not the ones sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust that she loved — white being the dress ladies wear only when they worship the gods?

And then his protest, the whole answer to everything she had not yet said: "Just as flame is in fire, so my love resides in thee, and thee only."
reflection: Krishna does not meet Satyabhama's jealousy with correction or a defense of his conduct; he slips past her guards, takes up the fan, and asks her why she is sad — the question of a lover, not a lord. The protest that his love dwells in her alone is all the more tender for coming while she is still turned away, still unwilling to look at him.
next_story_tease: The flower, it turned out, was not the wound; the wound was being left out — and Krishna answered it with a promise far larger than a single flower.
hero_scene: Krishna, fan in hand, catching Satyabhama's falling tears in his cupped hands as she sits on the edge of her bed with her face turned away and half-hidden in her veil, her handmaids kneeling silent with joined palms in the shadowed apartment of anger.
